title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 54–55
description: Units 54–55 audited against their illustrated teaching pages, exercises and answer key. Unit 54 covers adjectives, manner adverbs, and expressions with way; Unit 55 covers countable and uncountable nouns, singular agreement, collocations and quantity expressions. Original examples, Brazilian Portuguese translations and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was used to verify instructional targets in teaching pages, illustrations and exercises. Example sentences and explanations are original. The four Over to you words appear in the source as dictionary tasks; their countability explanations are supplementary guidance.

audit.scope: Direct inspection of Unit 54 teaching sections A–E and exercises 54.1–54.4; Unit 55 teaching sections A–C, illustrated examples, exercises 55.1–55.4 and Over to you. Answer key checked on printed p. 155 (PDF p. 156); each item reviewed for target accuracy, IPA, naturalness and translation.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA, primarily non-rhotic, reviewed item by item; source headword pronunciations and the textbook phonemic index are reference points. Connected speech and some multiword expressions admit variants.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Valid JSON and local structure/ID checks are not an application acceptance test. VocabLab 1.2 Lite import, browser text-to-speech and microphone, review scheduling, and backup/restore were not tested. Human editorial sign-off is still required.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Source teaching and exercise pages visually inspected alongside extracted text, published answer key checked, item-by-item linguistic and phonetic review, English-only metadata/notes and ID/schema-shape validation.
editorialReview.notes: All 105 pre-existing vocabulary IDs are retained. Some noun classifications in Over to you are dictionary-based educational extensions, not explanations printed by the source. No browser or application acceptance tests were executed.

units.title: Unit 54 — Manner
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 54. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: The new bus is fast, and it moves fast.
items.note: Fast can be an adjective (a fast car) or an adverb (go fast). Do not use fastly for this meaning.

items.example: This computer is slow today.
items.note: Slow is an adjective describing a person or thing. Use slowly as the standard adverb of manner.

items.example: Please walk slowly on the wet floor.
items.note: Slowly describes how an action happens: move slowly, speak slowly. It is formed from slow + -ly.

items.example: My neighbour has a fast car.
items.note: In a fast car, fast is an adjective modifying the noun car, as illustrated in section A.

items.example: We travelled in a slow car.
items.note: In a slow car, slow is an adjective; contrast the adverb in the car goes slowly.

items.example: These trains can go fast.
items.note: Fast modifies go here, even though it has no -ly ending. Contrast go slowly.

items.example: The old lift goes slowly.
items.note: Use slowly to say how someone or something moves. A slow car goes slowly.

items.example: Leah is a fast swimmer.
items.note: The noun swimmer is modified by the adjective fast. Exercise 54.1 contrasts this with swims fast.

items.example: My brother can swim fast.
items.note: Fast is an adverb in swim fast. Do not say swim fastly; this pattern is reinforced in exercise 54.1.

items.example: That radio is too loud.
items.note: Loud describes strong sound or noise. The music is too loud in the teaching illustration.

items.pt: em voz alta; de modo barulhento
items.example: The children laughed loudly outside.
items.note: Loudly is the regular manner adverb from loud. It describes how somebody speaks, sings or plays music.

items.example: The library is quiet in the morning.
items.note: Quiet means making little or no noise. It is an adjective; compare the adverb quietly.

items.example: Please close the door quietly.
items.note: Quietly is the adverb from quiet. It describes how somebody speaks or acts, not a person's character.

items.example: The television is too loud for the baby.
items.note: Too loud means louder than is acceptable or comfortable. Too can suggest a problem.

items.pt: falar baixinho; falar em voz baixa
items.example: We must speak quietly in the hospital.
items.note: Speak quietly uses an adverb to describe the way somebody speaks. Quiet is the adjective.

items.example: Our friends sometimes sing loudly.
items.note: Sing loudly uses an adverb after the action verb. Loud is the corresponding adjective.

items.pt: colocar música alta; tocar música em volume alto
items.example: Please do not play music loudly at night.
items.note: Exercise 54.2 reinforces play music loudly; do not replace the adverb with loud in the textbook pattern.

items.example: Mara is a good teacher.
items.note: Good is an adjective, as in a good driver. Use well as the corresponding manner adverb.

items.example: He had a bad day at work.
items.note: Bad is an adjective, as in a bad driver. Use badly as the corresponding manner adverb.

items.example: She sings well.
items.note: Well is the adverb corresponding to good when describing performance: drive well, speak well.

items.example: I played very badly yesterday.
items.note: Badly describes poor performance: drive badly, sing badly. Compare the adjective bad.

items.example: My father is a good driver.
items.note: Good describes the noun driver. The illustration contrasts a good driver with a bad driver.

items.example: I am not a bad driver.
items.note: Bad describes the noun driver. The illustration contrasts this with drives badly.

items.example: My sister drives well in heavy traffic.
items.note: Well describes how somebody drives, rather than the person or vehicle. Use drives well.

items.example: He drives badly when he is tired.
items.note: Badly describes how somebody drives. Use drives badly, not drives bad, in the teaching pattern.

items.example: I sing badly, but I enjoy music.
items.note: Sing badly describes poor singing performance; exercise 54.1 uses this contrast with a bad singer.

items.example: She speaks English well at work.
items.note: Use well after speaks English to describe language performance. Do not use good in this position.

items.example: My cousin is good at French.
items.note: Good at + subject or activity describes ability. Exercise 54.2 contrasts good at French with bad at German.

items.example: Your answer is right.
items.note: Right means correct in section D; it is the opposite of wrong in judgments about a sentence or answer.

items.example: That answer is wrong.
items.note: Wrong means incorrect; do not confuse it with badly, which describes the manner of an action.

items.example: I think you have the right answer.
items.note: A right answer is correct; exercise 54.2 includes the right answer. The is used for a specific one.

items.example: The first answer was wrong, so I tried again.
items.note: A wrong answer is incorrect; right and wrong here are adjectives modifying answer.

items.example: There is another way to open this box.
items.note: Way can mean a method or manner of doing something. Expressions with way are introduced in section E.

items.example: Our new neighbours are friendly.
items.note: Friendly describes a pleasant and kind manner. It is an adjective ending in -ly, not an adverb.

items.example: The man at the desk was unfriendly.
items.note: Unfriendly is the opposite of friendly. The negative prefix un- changes the meaning.

items.pt: de maneira amigável; de modo simpático
items.example: The receptionist spoke in a friendly way.
items.note: Use in a friendly way to describe someone's manner; do not form the nonstandard adverb friendlyly.

items.pt: de maneira pouco amigável; de modo antipático
items.example: He answered in an unfriendly way.
items.note: Use in an unfriendly way to describe an unpleasant manner. An precedes the vowel sound in unfriendly.

items.pt: a maneira correta; do jeito certo
items.example: Is this the right way to wash the window?
items.note: The right way means the correct method. The book also shows the right way to do it.

items.pt: a maneira errada; do jeito errado
items.example: I was trying to open the box the wrong way.
items.note: The wrong way means an incorrect method. Contrast the right way in section E.

items.example: Try to hold the camera in the right way.
items.note: Use in the right way when describing a method of doing an action; exercise 54.2 practises the article the.

items.pt: mostrar a alguém o jeito certo
items.example: Please show me the right way to clean it.
items.note: Show someone the right way is a teaching pattern; the person after show can be me, him, her or us.

items.example: The lights suddenly went out.
items.note: Suddenly means quickly and unexpectedly, not very slowly. Exercise 54.3 asks learners to check this meaning.

items.example: She spoke sadly about her old dog.
items.note: Sadly means in an unhappy or sorrowful way; its definition is confirmed by exercise 54.3.

items.example: The clock was working strangely.
items.note: Strangely means in an unusual or unexpected way, not in the normal way. Exercise 54.3 checks this sense.

items.example: He finished the exercise quickly.
items.note: Quickly means fast or without much delay, not very slowly. Exercise 54.3 contrasts it with the false definition.

items.example: I can easily read this sign.
items.note: Easily means without difficulty. It is an adverb of manner, as checked in exercise 54.3.

learningObjectives: Identify adjectives and manner adverbs in descriptions of people, actions and situations.
Distinguish fast as an adjective and adverb from slow and slowly, and recognise regular -ly formation.
Use loud/loudly and quiet/quietly naturally with music, speech and other actions.
Distinguish good/well and bad/badly; use adjectives to modify nouns and adverbs to describe actions.
Use right and wrong for correctness and build expressions with the right/wrong way.
Describe manner with in a friendly way and in an unfriendly way instead of the nonstandard form friendlyly.
Recognise suddenly, sadly, strangely, quickly and easily from the definition-checking exercise.

units.title: Unit 55 — Common uncountable nouns
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 55. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: Apple is a countable noun.
items.note: A countable noun can be counted and has singular and plural forms: an apple, four apples.

items.example: Money is an uncountable noun.
items.note: An uncountable noun is not normally counted as separate units in the sense taught here: some money, not three moneys.

items.example: I bought an apple for my lunch.
items.note: Apple is countable in this use: an apple, two apples. Contrast uncountable sugar.

items.example: We need four apples for this recipe.
items.note: Apples is the regular plural of apple; the illustration has four apples.

items.example: These shoes are too small.
items.note: Shoes is the plural of shoe, a countable noun; the page shows two shoes.

items.example: There are six plates in the cupboard.
items.note: Plates is the plural of plate, a countable noun; the illustration shows several plates.

items.example: Would you like some sugar in your tea?
items.note: Sugar is uncountable when referring to the ingredient generally. Say some sugar, not three sugars, in this use.

items.example: We have enough money for the tickets.
items.note: Money is uncountable in the ordinary general sense. Use some or enough money, not a money.

items.example: Your luggage is near the door.
items.note: Luggage is uncountable even for several bags or cases. Say this luggage, not these luggages.

items.pt: um pouco de açúcar; açúcar (quantidade não especificada)
items.example: Can I have some sugar, please?
items.note: Some is suitable with an uncountable noun in a request: some sugar; the teaching page models this use.

items.pt: algum dinheiro; um pouco de dinheiro
items.example: She saved some money for her holiday.
items.note: Some money refers to an unspecified amount. Money is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

items.example: This luggage belongs to my brother.
items.note: This luggage takes this and a singular verb, even if the luggage includes more than one bag.

items.example: Traffic is heavy on this road today.
items.note: Traffic is uncountable in the sense of vehicles on the road. Use the traffic is, not the traffic are.

items.example: The furniture in this room is new.
items.note: Furniture is uncountable when referring collectively to tables, chairs and similar objects. Not furnitures.

items.example: My teacher gave me some helpful advice.
items.note: Advice is an uncountable noun. Use some advice or a piece of advice, not an advice.

items.example: The website has useful information.
items.note: Information is uncountable, even if it consists of several facts. Not informations in this sense.

items.example: The news is good this morning.
items.note: News is uncountable and takes singular agreement despite ending in -s: the news is.

items.example: The weather is cold today.
items.note: Weather is uncountable for atmospheric conditions in general. Say terrible weather, not a terrible weather.

items.example: Accommodation is expensive near the beach.
items.note: Accommodation is normally uncountable for somewhere to stay in this British English use. Say some accommodation.

items.example: We opened the windows for some fresh air.
items.note: Air is uncountable in its ordinary sense. Fresh air is a common expression in section B.

items.example: There is a lot of work to do today.
items.note: Work is uncountable when it means effort or employment in general. Say hard work or look for work.

items.example: Travel is part of her job.
items.note: Travel is uncountable as a general activity. Air travel and rail travel are illustrated in section B.

items.example: There was bad traffic on the way home.
items.note: The teaching page says the traffic is bad; traffic remains uncountable and takes singular agreement.

items.example: We chose modern furniture for our office.
items.note: Modern furniture is the expression in the teaching illustration; furniture remains singular in agreement.

items.example: Can you give me some advice?
items.note: The pattern give someone some advice is taught directly and tested in exercise 55.4.

items.example: The guide gave us useful information.
items.note: Useful information is shown in section B. Information is uncountable and does not normally have a plural -s.

items.example: This is bad news for the team.
items.note: The page uses some bad news. News takes a singular verb: the news is, even for several reports.

items.example: We had terrible weather during our trip.
items.note: Terrible weather is a combination on the teaching page. Do not add an indefinite article before weather.

items.example: I like to get some fresh air after lunch.
items.note: Fresh air is an expression illustrated in section B. Use some fresh air, not a fresh air, in this sense.

items.example: Learning to swim was hard work for me.
items.note: Hard work means effortful activity. The teaching illustration relates it to studying.

items.example: Air travel can be tiring.
items.note: Air travel means travelling by plane. Travel is an uncountable noun in this expression.

items.example: Rail travel is popular in this region.
items.note: Rail travel means travelling by train. The teaching page contrasts rail travel with air travel.

items.example: We had rice and vegetables for lunch.
items.note: Rice is uncountable as food: some rice, a kilo of rice, not rices in the normal food sense.

items.example: Spaghetti is my favourite pasta.
items.note: Spaghetti is uncountable as a food name in this lesson. Use spaghetti is, not these spaghetti are.

items.example: There is some butter in the fridge.
items.note: Butter is uncountable when referring to the food substance. Use some butter.

items.example: We need bread for breakfast.
items.note: Bread is uncountable as a food name. Count loaves or slices, not breads, in the general sense taught here.

items.example: The milk is in the fridge.
items.note: Milk is uncountable as a liquid. Quantify it with litres, glasses or other containers.

items.example: Please give me some water.
items.note: Water is uncountable in its ordinary substance sense. Say some water or a litre of water.

items.example: I drink tea every morning.
items.note: Tea is uncountable when referring to the drink generally. A cup of tea is one serving.

items.example: My mother likes coffee with milk.
items.note: Coffee is uncountable in general use. A coffee can mean a serving, but that is not this lesson's focus.

items.example: I bought a loaf of bread at the bakery.
items.note: A loaf of bread specifies one unit of bread. Loaf is countable; bread remains uncountable.

items.example: We bought two loaves of bread for the picnic.
items.note: Two loaves of bread quantifies bread using the irregular plural of loaf: loaves, not loafs.

items.example: The shop ordered three litres of milk.
items.note: Three litres of milk quantifies an uncountable liquid. Litres is countable; milk stays uncountable.

items.example: We need a kilo of rice for the meal.
items.note: A kilo of rice gives the amount of rice by weight; rice remains uncountable.

items.example: My heavy luggage is upstairs.
items.note: Heavy luggage is a collocation in exercise 55.2. Luggage is not normally pluralised as luggages.

items.pt: pão escuro; pão de farinha integral (conforme o produto)
items.example: I would like some brown bread, please.
items.note: Brown bread is a collocation in exercise 55.2. Brown describes the type or colour of the bread.

items.example: We drank cold water after the walk.
items.note: Cold water is a collocation in exercise 55.2. Water remains uncountable.

items.example: Space travel may become cheaper in the future.
items.note: Space travel is a collocation in exercise 55.2. Travel is uncountable as an activity.

items.example: My friend is looking for work.
items.note: Look for work means try to find employment; the construction is reinforced in exercise 55.1.

items.example: Our coach often gives good advice.
items.note: Give advice is the natural verb–noun combination. Exercise 55.1 includes asking parents for advice.

items.pt: as notícias são/estão; a notícia é/está
items.example: The news is better today.
items.note: The news is uses singular agreement, even though news ends in -s. Exercises 55.3 and 55.4 reinforce this.

items.pt: os móveis são/estão; o mobiliário é/está
items.example: The furniture is very old.
items.note: The furniture is takes a singular verb. Exercise 55.3 tests the agreement pattern.

items.pt: o tempo está; as condições do tempo são
items.example: The weather is warmer today.
items.note: The weather is uses a singular verb. Exercise 55.4 also rejects a better weather in this meaning.

items.example: Accommodation is cheaper in winter.
items.note: Accommodation is uses singular agreement. Exercise 55.3 practises this pattern.

items.example: The spaghetti is ready.
items.note: Spaghetti is takes a singular verb as a food noun in this lesson. Do not say these spaghetti.

items.example: The equipment is new.
items.note: Equipment is listed for dictionary research in Over to you. It is generally uncountable: some equipment; this classification is an explanatory extension.

items.example: Would you like a biscuit?
items.note: Biscuit is listed for dictionary research in Over to you. It is countable: a biscuit, two biscuits; this classification is an explanatory extension.

items.example: My homework is on the table.
items.note: Homework is listed for dictionary research in Over to you. It is uncountable: some homework; this classification is an explanatory extension.

items.example: There are two vehicles outside.
items.note: Vehicle is listed for dictionary research in Over to you. It is countable: one vehicle, two vehicles; this classification is an explanatory extension.

learningObjectives: Distinguish countable and uncountable nouns using the illustrations and examples in the unit.
Use some and avoid inappropriate articles and plural -s with nouns such as advice, information, luggage and furniture.
Use singular verb agreement with news, furniture, accommodation, spaghetti and other uncountable nouns.
Recognise common uncountable nouns related to work, travel, weather and food.
Use common combinations such as useful information, heavy luggage, brown bread, cold water and space travel.
Quantify foods and drinks with loaves of bread, litres of milk and a kilo of rice.
Classify equipment, biscuit, homework and vehicle using a dictionary, as suggested by Over to you.
